question_en: A manufacturer operates two production plants: Plant 1 and Plant 2. After ten years, management restructures the company by closing Plant 2 and shifting its entire operations to Plant 1. All expenses, as well as any gains or losses, from the closure of Plant 2 are most appropriately be reported under:
explanation_en:
Most income statement information focuses on results from normal operations, since earnings and growth forecasts arise from how companies
perform their usual activities. A company may also have gains or losses from transactions falling outside its normal operations, such as unusual
or infrequent items or the discontinuation of a component of its business. Both GAAP and IFRS require special reporting treatment for such
items.
US GAAP and IFRS consider closing one of several production facilities (ie, restructuring) to be an unusual or infrequent item, reported as a part
of operating income. The company reports the unusual or infrequent item separately from other operating revenues and expenses on the income
statement.
The company is not discontinuing its operations entirely, but instead is closing one facility (Plant 2) and shifting all operations to the other facility
(Plant 1) (Choice B). Therefore any costs and gains (or losses) are considered restructuring costs captured under unusual or infrequent items,
rather than activities relating to discontinued operations.
(Choice A) After 2015, neither US GAAP nor IFRS recognize extraordinary items. Before then, an extraordinary item was defined as both
unusual and infrequent and was treated the same as discontinued operations.

question_en: A company has 10 million shares of common stock outstanding and has not issued or repurchased common stock this year. It issued 300,000 employee stock options several years ago, which are presently exercisable at $40 per share. The average market price per share for the company's stock this year is $30. It also paid dividends of $1 million on its nonconvertible preferred stock. If the company has a net income of $11 million this year, the company's reported EPS will be closest to:
explanation_en:
Employee stock options, if exercised, will increase the number of shares outstanding. This causes earnings per share (EPS) to decrease since
net income is divided by a larger number of shares. Employee stock options are dilutive securities. The general rule is that all dilutive securities
are converted to common stock or, in the case of options, exercised at the beginning of the period.
For employee stock options, this presumption of exercise is valid only if the stock's average market price exceeds the option's exercise price.
Exercising an option must make economic sense, which is not the case by paying $40 for a share worth $30. The options will not be exercised in
this case, so the weighted average number of shares will not change. Basic EPS is calculated as follows:
(Choice B) Under these assumptions, the options would not be exercised since it would be economically unsound to do so. If they were, the
treasury stock method would result in the company having 100,000 fewer shares outstanding, or 9.9 million weighted average number of shares
for the period. Dividing $10 million ($11 million net income − $1 million preferred dividend) by 9.9 million shares results in an EPS of $1.01.
(Choice C) Preferred dividends are paid from net income, so they are not available to the common shareholders. The EPS of $1.10 results from
neglecting to first subtract the preferred dividends from net income before dividing by the weighted average number of common shares.

question_en: At the end of its fiscal year, a company has net income of $8,750,000 and 1,000,000 weighted average common shares outstanding. It also has 200,000 shares of convertible preferred shares. Each preferred share pays a dividend of $15 per share and is convertible into two shares of the company's common stock. There are no other potentially dilutive securities. The company would most appropriately report diluted earnings per share of:
explanation_en:
Diluted EPS is calculated using the if-converted method if a company issues convertible preferred shares. This method assumes the
convertible preferred shares are converted into common shares at the beginning of the period.
Here, preferred dividends are $3,000,000 (200,000 shares × $15 per share dividend). Earnings available to common shareholders are lower in
the basic EPS ($5.75 million) than the if-converted method ($8.75 million). The additional number of shares considered outstanding using the if-
converted method is 400,000 (2 common shares per preferred share × 200,000 preferred shares).
Calculated diluted EPS using the if-converted method is greater than basic EPS ($6.25 vs. $5.75). This means the convertible security is
antidilutive. Under IFRS and GAAP, antidilutive securities are excluded from the diluted EPS calculation since it must reflect the maximum
potential dilution from potentially dilutive securities. When a company has antidilutive securities, reported diluted EPS is equal to basic EPS
($5.75).

question_en: Under IFRS, a company reporting bad debt expense should most appropriately:
option_a: write off the receivable when the customer fails to pay and recognize the write-off as a bad debt expense.
option_b: multiply the company's credit sales by its historical percentage of uncollectible receivables, and report that result as an operating expense.
option_c: multiply the company's average accounts receivable by the historical percentage of
explanation_en:
In general, an expense should be recognized in the same period in which the revenue associated with the expense was earned (ie, matching
principle). Sales on credit are reported as revenue in the period they were made. If the company has a history of being unable to collect all its
credit sales, then both IFRS and US GAAP require it to report a bad debt expense as an operating expense for that period.
Neither IFRS nor US GAAP mandate a specific methodology that a company must employ to estimate its bad debt expense. Several methods are
acceptable, such as a percentage of uncollectible accounts that is based on overall sales, overall credit sales, or delinquent credit sales. The
only requirements are that:
the company use the method consistently; and
the method fairly reflects a reasonable assessment of the company's bad debt history.
(Choice A) This is known as the direct write-off method. It violates the matching principle and neither IFRS nor US GAAP permit it to be used.
(Choice C) An operating expense is deducted from gross profit to calculate earnings before interest and taxes. Deducting it from revenues to
calculate gross profit will distort gross profit margins.

question_en: XYZ Corporation has 10 million shares of common stock outstanding and has not issued or repurchased common stock this year. Several years ago, it issued $10 million in bonds with 1,000,000 warrants attached. Each warrant allows the holder to purchase one share of XYZ common stock for $30. The average market price per share for XYZ stock this year is $40. It also paid dividends of $1 million on its nonconvertible preferred stock. If XYZ has a net income of $16 million this year, the diluted earnings per share that XYZ will report is closest to:
explanation_en:
A warrant is essentially an option allowing the holder of the warrant the right to purchase shares of common stock at a predetermined price.
Exercising a warrant causes the number of common shares outstanding to increase. This increase usually causes the company's earnings-per-
share (EPS) to decrease, so warrants are dilutive securities.
When calculating EPS, warrants are treated as having been exercised at the earlier of the beginning of the accounting period, if the warrants
were then outstanding, or the date of issuance. Both IFRS and GAAP require companies to use the treasury stock method for calculating the
effect of warrants on EPS. An example of XYZ's use of the treasury stock method is shown below.
A key assumption underlying the treasury stock method is that the average market price of the stock is more than the exercise price, so the
proceeds will purchase fewer shares than were issued from the warrants' exercise. The resulting weighted average is then used to calculate
diluted EPS. An example of XYZ's use of the treasury stock method is shown below.
(Choice A) $1.36 is obtained when the denominator is increased by the total number of shares issued from the warrants' exercise (1,000,000)
instead of the net shares added (250,000).
(Choice C) $1.56 results from neglecting to subtract the preferred dividend from net income in the numerator.

question_en: In 20X9 a publicly traded corporation reported $10 million in net income. The information concerning its common shares outstanding is shown below: The company also has 500,000 shares of nonconvertible preferred stock, which have been outstanding the entire year. The annual dividend for each share of preferred stock is $5.00, which has been paid. The basic earnings per share (EPS) for this company in 20X9 is closest to:
explanation_en:
Basic earnings per share (EPS) divides a company's net income by the number of shares of common stock outstanding. Scaling net income on a
per-share basis provides a better means to compare net income across time periods. Basic EPS assumes that the company has not issued other
securities, such as convertible debt, that can be converted into common stock.
Dividends on all classes of stock are paid from net income but since EPS applies only to common shares, net income must be adjusted by
subtracting dividends paid to preferred shareholders. Adjusting for preferred dividends accurately reflects the portion of income that is available to
common shareholders. In this question, the company's preferred dividends totaled $2.5 million (500,000 shares × $5 / share), so the EPS
numerator becomes $10 million − $2.5 million = $7.5 million.

question_en: A manufacturer will voluntarily increase the useful lives of several different types of equipment it uses in its manufacturing process. The change will be effective for the current year. To account for this change in its financial statements, the company is most likely required to:
option_a: restate net income reported in all prior financial statements.
option_b: explain the change in the footnotes but not restate prior earnings.
option_c: restate net income for prior periods if it determines that the change is material.
explanation_en:
Treatment of accounting changes
(identical under US GAAP and IFRS)
Changes in accounting policies Changes in accounting estimates
Imposed on companies by accounting bodies Apply mostly to changes in useful lives
Require retroactive earnings restatement Voluntary by companies
Applicable to all firms No retroactive restatement
An accounting change is a type of nonrecurring or nonoperating item that may require special treatment on a company's income statement.
Changes in accounting policies occur when IFRS or US GAAP make changes to their standards. Policy changes affect all companies that must
adhere to the standards and require that they retroactively apply the changes by restating prior earnings from prior periods.
By contrast, changes in accounting estimates are voluntarily undertaken by individual companies. These mostly apply to changes in the
estimated useful lives of long-term assets and result from a company's determination that prior estimates of useful life are no longer valid due to
changed circumstances. Companies apply these changes prospectively; they disclose the change in the footnotes to their financial statements,
but no restatement is required.
Neither IFRS nor US GAAP required the company in this question to change their useful life estimates by changing the relevant accounting
standards. The company's changes are properly classified as changes in estimates rather than changes in policy. The company will apply the
new depreciation expenses going forward and disclose the changes in the footnotes to its financial statements.
(Choices A) Restatement is required only when the change results from a change in accounting policy rather than a change in accounting
estimates.
(Choice C) When accounting standards change, companies must change their accounting policies to comply with the updated standards.
Companies are not allowed to decide for themselves whether to comply by determining whether the change is "material."

question_en: A company sells cloud-based accounting software. A 12-month subscription costs $3,000 payable in advance. If this company reports under IFRS standards, how much revenue will it recognize for the 4th month of each subscription?
explanation_en:
Accrual accounting Cash accounting
Revenue is earned
Seller substantially completes all of its obligations
Goods delivered
Revenue recognition Cash is received
Services provided
Seller (usually) completes obligations before receiving payment
Example: Payment is due 30 days after invoice
Expense is incurred
Mirror image of revenue recognition
Expense recognition Cash is paid
Goods received
Services accepted or consumed
A key concept of accrual accounting is that revenue is recognized when it is earned. The seller earns revenue from a sale when it has
substantially fulfilled all its obligations under the terms of the sale. The seller then reports the earned revenue. Under accrual accounting, revenue
recognition does not depend on whether the seller receives payment.
The company in this question provides its subscribers with access for one year following the subscriber's payment, so it has received payment
before it has completed its obligation. However, accounting standards require that it recognize a prorated amount of the subscription price as
revenue each month during the subscription period. Accordingly, the company will recognize 1/12th of the total subscription price each month, or
$3,000 / 12 = $250.
Note that the answer is the same whether the seller reports under IFRS or US GAAP accounting standards.
(Choice A) The company's obligation can be viewed as 12 separate monthly contracts. At the end of every month, it will have earned the
prorated share of the subscription price and will recognize the revenue associated with that month. Accounting standards do not permit the
company to delay any revenue recognition until the end of the entire subscription period. Such a delay would distort its financial picture.
(Choice C) $1,000 is the cumulative amount of income earned by the end of Month 4, not the amount earned solely for Month 4.

question_en: A company finalizes a contract to sell a product that will be delivered to the customer 2 months from today. The customer will pay the full amount of the contract next month. If the company expects no problems in delivering the product or receiving payments, then it will most appropriately recognize revenue:
explanation_en:
Accrual accounting Cash accounting
Revenue is earned
Seller substantially completes all of its obligations
Goods delivered
Revenue recognition Cash is received
Services provided
Seller (usually) completes obligations before receiving payment
Example: Payment is due 30 days after invoice
Expense is incurred
Mirror image of revenue recognition
Expense recognition Cash is paid
Goods received
Services accepted or consumed
Under both IFRS and US GAAP, revenue is recognized when it is earned, independent of when cash is received, as under accrual accounting.
The seller earns revenue from a sale when it has satisfied its performance obligations, effectively transferring the risk and rewards of
ownership. This typically occurs when a good or service is delivered to the buyer.
Under accrual accounting, the recognition of revenue occurs independently of when the seller receives cash for the sale, which is when the
revenue is recognized in cash basis accounting (Choice B). In accrual accounting, when a company delivers goods or services at a different time
from when it receives cash, it creates an asset or liability on its balance sheet to account for the different events of recognizing revenue and
receiving cash.
In this scenario, the company finalized a contract to deliver a product 2 months from today. Therefore, no revenue is recognized immediately
since no product is delivered immediately (Choice A). Revenue will be recognized on the income statement when the delivery is made in 2
months since that is when the risk and rewards of ownership are transferred.

option_c: Smaller proportion of selling, general, and administrative expenses
explanation_en:
Common-size income statements present each statement item as a percentage of total revenue. This allows analysts to compare companies
of different sizes, view performance trends over time, and identify differences or changes in the companies' strategies.
In this scenario, the common-size income statement is calculated as follows:

question_en: On January 1, 20X8, Company Z issued convertible preferred stock that pays a dividend. Other than common stock, Company Z has issued no other securities. When an analyst calculated its basic and diluted earnings per share (EPS) for the year, the analyst found that basic EPS was $0.50 and diluted EPS was $0.55. Company Z should treat the convertible stock as:
option_a: dilutive and report only diluted EPS.
option_b: antidilutive and report only basic EPS.
option_c: dilutive and report both diluted EPS and basic EPS.
explanation_en:
Both US GAAP and IFRS require companies that have convertible securities in their capital structure (ie, complex structure) to calculate and
report both basic earnings per share (EPS) and diluted EPS. Diluted EPS assumes that all convertible securities were converted to common stock
at the beginning of the period. Conversion usually causes EPS to be lower due to the increased number of shares over which net income is
apportioned.
When diluted EPS is greater than basic EPS, the convertible securities are described as antidilutive. Both GAAP and IFRS require a company to
exclude antidilutive securities from EPS calculations and report only the lower EPS figure (ie, basic EPS). Company Z has both convertible
preferred and common stock, but since its diluted EPS is $0.05 greater than basic EPS, the convertible preferred stock is antidilutive. Therefore,
Company Z will report only the basic EPS of $0.50 for the year.
(Choice A) The convertible preferred stock is antidilutive, so Company Z will report only basic EPS.
(Choice C) The convertible preferred stock is antidilutive, but GAAP and IFRS both require Company Z to report basic, not diluted, EPS.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.02 Analyzing Income Statements - Answers.pdf
question_en: A company has issued convertible bonds and has no other dilutive securities outstanding. If the convertible bonds are antidilutive, the impact on reported basic and diluted earnings per share (EPS) is most likely that:
option_c: both basic and diluted EPS are impacted.
explanation_en:
IFRS and US GAAP require companies to report basic and diluted earnings per share (EPS). Basic EPS is calculated by dividing the firm's
income available to common shareholders (ie, net income less preferred dividends) by its weighted average number of common shares. Basic
EPS ignores any impact from potentially dilutive convertible securities. If the company has a simple capital structure with no convertible
securities, then diluted EPS is equal to basic EPS.
If the company has a complex capital structure, and if its convertible securities are dilutive, then diluted EPS is less than basic EPS. Accounting
standards treat all dilutive convertible securities as if they are converted to common stock at the beginning of the year. In general, this
hypothetical conversion increases the number of shares outstanding, which makes diluted EPS less than basic EPS.
In some cases, conversion results in fewer common shares outstanding and/or in more earnings available to common shareholders, which causes
calculated diluted EPS to be greater than basic EPS. In such cases, the securities are antidilutive. Since companies should report the most
conservative (ie, lowest) figure for EPS, if basic EPS is lower than calculated diluted EPS, then reported diluted EPS is equal to basic EPS. Both
basic and diluted EPS effectively ignore any impact from antidilutive securities (Choices A and C).

question_en: A company will report net income of €30 million this fiscal year ending 31 December. It began the year with 40 million common shares and neither issued nor repurchased common shares during the year. On July 1, the firm sold 100,000 shares of convertible preferred stock for €50 per share. The shares carry a 5% dividend and are immediately convertible into 20 shares of common stock. The effective tax rate is 40%. The company's diluted EPS for the year is closest to:
explanation_en:
A corporation must report basic earnings per share (EPS) as well as diluted EPS if its capital structure includes securities that can be
converted into common shares. If converted, such securities increase the number of shares outstanding, so net income is divided by more
shares, resulting in a lower per-share figure.
For calculating diluted EPS, convertible preferred stock is assumed to have been converted to common stock (ie, if-converted method) at the
beginning of the period.
The if-converted method treats the preferred stock as though it never existed, so the company will not have to pay dividends on it. For diluted
EPS, the dividends that would have been paid are added back to net income, which increases the numerator. Firm B's adjustments from basic to
diluted EPS are shown below:
(Choice B) The preferred dividends were added back to net income, so the numerator is correct, but the weighted average number of shares was
calculated as if the preferred stock had been converted as of the date it was issued (July 1), rather than the beginning of the period (January 1).
This would cause the additional shares to be 1,000,000 instead of 2,000,000, and the diluted EPS to be approximately 0.73.
(Choice C) 0.74 is closest to the company's basic EPS, not its diluted EPS.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.02 Analyzing Income Statements - Answers.pdf
question_en: A company just sold a warehouse that it no longer uses. The sale price was $4 million payable in equal installments over four years. The buyer has paid the first installment of $1 million and is expected to make the remaining payments on time. The company carried the warehouse on its balance sheet at its net book value of $6 million. This year, the company will most appropriately recognize a loss of:
explanation_en:
Under the accrual accounting method, revenues are generally recognized in the accounting period they are earned, and any associated gains or
losses are also recognized in the same period. A seller earns the revenue by performing all its requirements under a contract. One exception to
the general rule is for installment sales, in which the seller receives payments over more than one accounting period.
With installments, the seller recognizes a prorated amount of the total profit from the sale each year. However, the installment sales exception
applies only when the seller has a gain from the sale. If the sale is made at a loss, then the entire loss is realized immediately and recognized
in the period of the sale.
(Choice A) Although the company's loss may exceed $2 million if the buyer defaults on payments, the firm at this point has no reason to assume
that the buyer will default. There is no uncertainty surrounding the current amount of the company's loss of $2 million; therefore, the firm must
immediately realize and recognize the loss.
(Choice B) The installment sales exception does not apply to sales made at a loss, and the seller cannot prorate the loss over the installment
period.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.02 Analyzing Income Statements - Answers.pdf
question_en:
An analyst gathers the following information about a company for the most recent fiscal year:

- annual net income: HKD 500 million
- weighted average common shares outstanding: 250 million
- convertible debt outstanding: HKD 100 million at 9% interest, convertible into 10 million common shares
- tax rate: 33.33%

If there are no other dilutive securities, then diluted EPS (in HKD) is closest to:
explanation_en:
Companies with complex capital structures (ie, potentially dilutive securities) may report a diluted earnings per share (EPS) that is different
from its basic EPS. Dilutive securities (eg, convertible preferred stock, convertible debt, employee stock options) are convertible into shares of
common stock. Companies issue additional common shares upon conversion, creating more outstanding shares and thus diluting EPS. Using
the if-converted method, diluted EPS is calculated assuming that conversion occurred at the beginning of the period.
Assuming the company in this scenario converted its preferred shares to common shares at the beginning of the period, it would not have paid
preferred dividends of $2 million. Therefore, the diluted EPS numerator includes only net income. Furthermore, the company would have issued
10 million additional common shares, increasing the denominator and reducing the EPS to $0.45.
(Choice B) 0.48 is the basic EPS.
(Choice C) 0.49 results from not applying the 5-to-1 conversion ratio to each preferred share.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.03 Analyzing Balance Sheets - Answers.pdf
question_en: A company reported a goodwill impairment of USD 800 million for the first quarter ending 20X2. Based on only this information, it is most likely that:
option_a: net income was unaffected by the impairment.
option_b: investing cash flow was reduced by the amount of impairment.
option_c: management overpaid for one or more acquisitions in the past.
explanation_en: Goodwill is the difference between the price an acquiring company pays for a target company and the fair market value of the target company's identifiable net assets (ie, fair value of assets minus fair value of liabilities). Goodwill impairments result from the loss of value of those assets, which ultimately did not live up to initial expectations and must be written down. There may be many reasons (eg, a decline in competitiveness, political instability) why the acquisition, and thus the goodwill it generated, has not maintained its value. In hindsight, the assets have proven to be less valuable than expected, and it is likely that management overpaid for them. Goodwill is capitalized on the acquiring company's balance sheet as a noncurrent intangible asset. Since it has no finite life, it is not amortized; instead, it is evaluated annually for possible impairment. If an impairment is deemed appropriate, an impairment loss affects the financial statements in the period when it is identified, reducing total assets and flowing through the income statement, impacting earnings as a noncash charge. (Choice A) Net income is directly affected by goodwill impairment since a charge must be taken against income in the current period. (Choice B) Goodwill impairment is a noncash charge and therefore does not impact the cash flow statement.

question_en: An analyst compiles the following common-size balance sheet items for a company: Based only on the data above, the most appropriate conclusion the analyst can draw is that compared to 20X8, in 20X9 the company has:
explanation_en: Required disclosures of property, plant, and equipment (PPE) vary between IFRS and US GAAP. Under US GAAP, required disclosures are much less detailed as compared to IFRS. PPE includes tangible assets with useful lives of greater than one year. The costs (ie, measurement base) to obtain them are capitalized. Each year, part of the PPE cost is expensed as depreciation. Disclosures help analysts identify how different companies determine original costs and calculate depreciation expenses. The disclosure of assets' useful lives is required exclusively under IFRS. Useful life is an estimate of the time remaining in which an asset continues to provide economic benefit (eg, generate revenue). (Choice B) Both IFRS and US GAAP require the disclosure of the gross carrying amount. The gross carrying amount is the value of an asset prior to accounting for deprecation. (Choice C) The disclosure of estimated depreciation over the next five years is required under US GAAP, not IFRS.

question_en:
An analyst forecasts the upcoming year's fixed charge coverage ratio (FCCR) to be 2. Within the forecast:

- EBIT is AUD 10 million
- tax expense is AUD 1.5 million
- and interest expense is AUD 4 million

The forecasted lease amount (in AUD millions) is closest to:
explanation_en: The units-of-production depreciation method expenses an asset's cost based on its use during each period. Depreciation expense is calculated by multiplying the units produced each year by the depreciable unit cost, which is calculated as the asset's depreciable value (ie, initial cost less salvage value) divided by the total number of units expected to be produced over the asset's life. The depreciable unit cost is constant since the asset's cost is known, and the salvage value and the total number of units expected to be produced are estimated at the beginning of the asset's life (Choice C). Therefore, the only variable that can change the depreciation expense will be the actual number of units produced. Using the units-of-production method, if the depreciation expense increases each year, the number of units produced is also expected to grow. (Choice B) Net margin (ie, net profit margin) is a measure of profitability, and it increases only if profit increases or revenue decreases. In this scenario, although production and COGS are expected to grow, that does not suggest the net margin will increase.

question_en: Which of the following is most likely a disclosure for PPE that is required under IFRS but not under US GAAP?
option_c: Estimated depreciation over the next five years
explanation_en:
Required disclosures of property, plant, and equipment (PPE) vary between IFRS and US GAAP. Under US GAAP, required disclosures are
much less detailed as compared to IFRS. PPE includes tangible assets with useful lives of greater than one year. The costs (ie, measurement
base) to obtain them are capitalized. Each year, part of the PPE cost is expensed as depreciation. Disclosures help analysts identify how different
companies determine original costs and calculate depreciation expenses.
The disclosure of assets' useful lives is required exclusively under IFRS. Useful life is an estimate of the time remaining in which an asset
continues to provide economic benefit (eg, generate revenue).
(Choice B) Both IFRS and US GAAP require the disclosure of the gross carrying amount. The gross carrying amount is the value of an asset
prior to accounting for deprecation.
(Choice C) The disclosure of estimated depreciation over the next five years is required under US GAAP, not IFRS.

question_en: An airline company reports the following information for 20X8: The fixed charge coverage ratio for 20X8 is closest to:
explanation_en:
Solvency ratios evaluate a company's ability to satisfy its long-term debt obligations. Coverage ratios such as the fixed charge coverage ratio
are one category of solvency ratios. Coverage ratios focus on income statement items and cash from operations (CFO) and illustrate a company's
ability to satisfy periodic payments related to debt and debt-like obligations such as leases.
Lease payments and interest on debt are two common types of fixed charges. The fixed charge coverage ratio measures the company's ability to
satisfy its fixed obligations from operating earnings. The company's fixed charge coverage ratio is shown below:
(Choice A) 1.29 results from using net income instead of EBIT to calculate the fixed charge coverage ratio.
(Choice C) 1.88 is the interest coverage ratio, which does not include lease payments.
